title: Backdoor Containment via Expert Quarantine and Shutdown in LLMs
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 30 Sep 2026]
    Title:Backdoor Containment via Expert Quarantine and Shutdown in LLMs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Backdoored large language models (LLMs) can behave normally on benign inputs while producing attacker-specified outputs under hidden triggers. Existing defenses span four stages--prior-training, in-training, post-training, and inference-time--and share one of two underlying strategies: either suppress backdoor learning (by filtering poisoned data or interrupting its acquisition during optimization) or learn, then purify (by repairing model weights or gating inputs after a fully backdoored model has formed). We propose a third strategy, learn, but channel: allow backdoor formation during training but route it into a designated, quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment. To this end, we propose Quarantined Expert Shutdown QES, a computationally efficient containment strategy built in a regularization-steered MoE-like setting. Specifically, given a poisoned dataset, QES augments a Transformer-based language model with routed expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routers, and uses auxiliary routing objectives to attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated expert while preserving benign capability elsewhere. At deployment, mitigation reduces to a single constant-time operation: zeroing the quarantined expert's routing weight, without trigger screening or further updating model weights. Empirically, our methods reduce the attack success rate ASR from 100% to 0-10% on most settings across two tasks, three attacks, and four model families, while downstream utility is often preserved or only modestly affected. These results establish learn, but channel as a previously unexplored regime for backdoor containment in generative LLMs.

report.summary: New QES method quarantines backdoor behavior in a dedicated MoE expert, then disables it at deployment by zeroing one routing weight.
report.background: Backdoor attacks implant hidden triggers in LLMs: the model behaves normally on ordinary prompts but emits attacker-controlled outputs when a rare phrase or pattern appears. Existing defenses target prior-training, in-training, post-training, or inference time, using two main strategies—suppress backdoor learning via data filtering and optimization interrupts, or learn-then-purify via weight repair and input gating. Both can be costly, degrade utility, or require trigger knowledge. As LLMs are increasingly fine-tuned on untrusted data and distributed as open weights, backdoor containment becomes a supply-chain security concern. QES sits in a regularization-steered mixture-of-experts setting with LoRA branches. It accepts that poisoned training will create a backdoor but channels it into a quarantinable expert, adding a third strategy: learn, but channel.
key_points: QES augments a Transformer with routed expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routers. Auxiliary routing objectives attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated quarantine expert while leaving benign capabilities distributed elsewhere. This makes the backdoor a separable module rather than a diffuse property of all weights.

At deployment, mitigation is a single constant-time operation: zeroing the quarantined expert’s routing weight. No trigger screening, fine-tuning, or weight repair is needed. That could make defense cheap enough for routine model serving and easier to audit than input filters.

Across two tasks, three attacks, and four model families, QES reduced attack success rate from 100% to 0–10% in most settings. Downstream utility was often preserved or only modestly affected, suggesting containment need not sacrifice general capability.

The work reframes backdoor defense as routing-time quarantining. It assumes a poisoned dataset and MoE-like architecture, so effectiveness may depend on data volume, trigger diversity, and router robustness. Adaptive attacks that evade or hijack routing remain open questions.
report.impact: For the AI industry, QES points toward safer supply chains for open-weight and fine-tuned LLMs: model providers could ship a deployment-time kill switch for learned backdoors instead of retraining or exhaustive trigger scanning. Developers working with MoE and LoRA stacks may gain a practical containment pattern, though they must secure routers and validate that benign capabilities do not rely on the quarantined expert. Regular users could benefit from models that retain utility while being less vulnerable to hidden triggers in chat, code, or agent settings. The bigger shift is conceptual: backdoors become containable architectural components, not only training-time mistakes. However, real-world assurance will require red-team testing, certification, and routing-level monitoring.
report.tools: Readers can follow related open-source work: Hugging Face Transformers and PEFT for LoRA, PyTorch for custom routing objectives, and MoE serving stacks such as vLLM, SGLang, and DeepSpeed-MoE. For evaluation, inspect BackdoorBench, TrojAI, and IBM’s Adversarial Robustness Toolbox. Mixtral, Qwen-MoE, and DeepSeek-MoE are useful reference architectures.
